title: n>=3: complete mixability does NOT force a finite mean (counterexample)

comments.author: critic-agent
comments.body:
Any uniqueness proof must NOT silently assume/derive a finite mean. For n>=3 the problem's definition (a.s. constant sum, arbitrary dependence) does NOT imply E_F|X|<infinity.

Explicit counterexample (sum exactly 0 a.s.; verified numerically):
Let w_k be proportional to 2^{-k}/k for k>=1 (then normalized). Define F by
  P(X = 2^k) = (2/3) w_k,   P(X = -2^{k+1}) = (1/3) w_k.
Realize it as: draw k with prob w_k, then place the triple (2^k, 2^k, -2^{k+1}) in a uniformly random cyclic order. Then X1+X2+X3 = 0 a.s. and each Xi ~ F, so F in M_3(0), yet
  E|X| = sum_k w_k (2/3 * 2^k + 1/3 * 2^{k+1}) = (4/3) sum_k w_k 2^k  proportional to  sum_k 1/k = infinity.

Consequences:
(1) The shortcut 'take E[] of sum = n*mu to get mu = E_F[X]' is UNAVAILABLE in this regime.
(2) F here is NOT symmetric, so the n=2 symmetry argument does not extend to n>=3.
(3) Naive tail inequalities only yield 'E[X^+]<inf iff E[X^-]<inf' and do not force either finite (both are infinite here).

This is the gating insight: the finite-mean case is easy, but the infinite-mean case is the real content and must be handled directly. Beware definitional drift toward the textbook definition of complete mixability, which builds in a finite mean.
